articles.body_html:
Are AI models running directly in the browser finally good enough to use in production? Let's find out! 😉

It's been a week since my talk at FrontKon in Prague. As I mentioned before, it was fantastic! I'm adding a few photos below, just to prove that I actually speak at conferences and don't just make these things up. 😀

My talk was titled "Your Browser Is a Compute Platform (And You're Using It for Forms)", and I showed how we can use WebAssembly and WebGPU to perform advanced computations directly in the browser. I was a little concerned to discover that, out of everyone in the audience, maybe three or four people had even heard of WebGPU! And that's a shame, because WebGPU can accelerate certain types of parallel computations by tens of times compared to CPU-based implementations.

But okay, at least the people at FrontKon know what WebGPU is now. 😁 And if you'd like a talk about this at your conference, feel free to reach out! Especially if your conference happens to take place in a particularly attractive tourist destination. 😀

Why I'm Revisiting Browser AI

After a conference, I traditionally prepare a blog post related to my talk. However, since I've already written about WebAssembly and WebGPU many times, today I'd like to approach the topic from a different angle. Namely, let's take a look at the current state of AI models running directly in the browser, which, of course, make extensive use of these technologies. 🙂

Browser-based AI models are a fascinating concept. No inference API calls. No network round trips to an AI backend. No worrying that your users will consume too many tokens, because you're not paying for them! But of course, local inference still takes time, and downloading the model in the first place can take a while.

Another advantage is that these models can work offline once they've been downloaded and cached by the browser, provided the application itself supports offline operation.

And that also brings a significant privacy benefit: inference happens directly on the user's device, so their data doesn't need to be sent to an external AI service.

However, as you can probably imagine, these are relatively small models. We're not going to run a massive frontier-scale model in a typical browser tab.

So the question is: how useful are these smaller models, really?

Some of you may remember that I experimented with browser-based AI models about a year ago. Back then, we were mostly laughing that they were a fun curiosity, but not much more than that.

But I've been following people from Hugging Face who work on Transformers.js on LinkedIn, and every now and then, their demos would appear in my feed. At first glance, some of them looked genuinely impressive. You know, practically spaceships running inside a browser. 😉

So before FrontKon, I decided to take another look at what they had to offer. And it turned out that after upgrading Transformers.js to version 4.3.1, which I used for these experiments, and trying some newer models, the results were genuinely impressive!

Of course, Transformers.js isn't the only option for running AI models in the browser. There are other libraries and runtimes, but I really like Transformers.js, and I think it's a pretty representative example of what this technology can achieve today.

At the same time, I don't work for Hugging Face, and nobody is paying me to sell you a spaceship in your browser. So I'll tell you what browser-based AI models can actually do today, what works well, and what still doesn't.

And even better, you can explore the code and try everything yourself!

GitHub: https://github.com/sylwia-lask/practical-browser-ai

Live demo: https://sylwia-lask.github.io/practical-browser-ai

If you like the project, please give it a star on GitHub. I'm collecting them! 😀

Can We Actually Use This in Production?

For these demos, I wanted to focus on practical applications. More specifically, I wanted to find out how we could use browser-based AI today, right now, in real production applications.

So is this technology worth paying attention to? In my opinion, absolutely!

But!

I probably wouldn't build a mission-critical system that depends entirely on these models working perfectly. 😉 Instead, I'd treat them as interesting, optional enhancements to existing application features, especially in areas like e-commerce, accessibility, and customer support.

The application itself is nothing particularly exotic, by the way. It's a regular React application written in TypeScript, using Web Workers to run model inference without blocking the main UI thread.

The models are loaded on demand, so you don't need to download all five of them just to open the application. The inference runs locally through Transformers.js, using WebGPU where supported and WebAssembly-based CPU execution where a fallback is available.

No AI backend involved!

Let's see what I managed to build. And at the end, I'll share my thoughts on the limitations of these models.

One more thing: these aren't browser-based AI agents yet. They're simply applications using local AI models for specific tasks. But give me a few more weeks, and you'll see agents running in the browser on my blog too!

1. Background Remover

One of the things I particularly appreciate about browser-based AI is that it's not limited to text generation. I love working with multimodal AI!

In this demo, a small model called RMBG-1.4, with approximately 44 million parameters, does a really impressive job of separating an object from its background. 🙂 The model itself is only about 170 MB to download in the configuration I'm using.

As you can see, we can then save the result as a transparent PNG, and it works surprisingly well!

I can easily imagine this as an additional feature on auction websites or e-commerce platforms.

Imagine someone trying to sell a product but only having a photo like my example. Instead of requiring them to use an external image-editing service, we could simply offer a background removal button directly in the application.

And the photo doesn't even need to leave their device. Pretty cool, isn't it?

One practical note: RMBG-1.4 comes with licensing conditions that should be checked before commercial deployment. So while the technical concept is very promising for e-commerce, you should always verify the model's license before shipping it.

2. Alt Text Generator

I've always felt that AI could become another useful layer of accessibility, if we use it properly.

This demo uses Florence-2-base-ft, a vision model with approximately 230 million parameters, to generate descriptions of images.

Imagine that you're uploading an image to DEV, for example. Instead of having to write an alt text description from scratch, you could use a model like this to generate a suggestion automatically. Especially when you really don't feel like describing what's in the picture!

Of course, the generated description should still be reviewed and edited by a human. Good alt text isn't just about identifying objects in an image. It also depends on the context and purpose of that image.

The model doesn't necessarily understand why you're using the picture, and it can occasionally miss or invent details. Still, as an accessibility assistant, I think this is a very promising approach.

There's also an option to provide additional context, but don't expect too much from it. In my implementation, the extra text is simply appended to the generated description rather than genuinely influencing what the model sees or understands. I'll explain why I wasn't satisfied with this approach later in the article.

For reference, the model download is roughly 350–450 MB, depending on the precision supported by the device.

3. Smart Ticket Creator

Oh, this one is my dream feature! I describe what's wrong in completely natural, messy language, and the model turns it into a structured ticket that I can send to support. 😀

The model I ended up using is Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, a small language model with approximately 500 million parameters. In my configuration, its quantized weights require a download of around 786 MB, plus tokenizer files.

And I have to admit something. When I started implementing this feature, I thought it would be the easiest one! Seriously. How difficult could it be for a language model to turn a complaint into a structured ticket?

Well... Apparently, quite difficult! I spent much more time than expected trying different models and getting them to produce the output I actually needed.

The main challenge wasn't just understanding the complaint. It was producing a consistent, structured response with the correct fields, without inventing information or returning malformed JSON. Eventually, I got it working using a carefully designed prompt, output parsing, and schema validation with Zod.

The generated ticket is editable, so the user can review everything before copying or submitting it. And I think that's exactly the kind of approach that makes sense for production: let the AI do the boring initial work, but keep the human in control.

4. Semantic Search

Now, this is where small models really shine! For this demo, I implemented semantic search over a collection of support tickets.

Instead of looking for matching keywords, the application searches for tickets with a similar meaning. And, of course, I also included a traditional keyword search so you can compare the results yourself.

I'm using all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a small embedding model with approximately 22 million parameters. Depending on the backend, its model weights are only about 23 MB for the quantized CPU version or 90 MB for the WebGPU version.

And it works really well! The model is fast, and the results are genuinely useful.

Under the hood, it converts the tickets and the search query into numerical vectors, then compares them using cosine similarity. No generative LLM is needed here.

In fact, that's one of the most interesting lessons from these experiments: sometimes a small, specialized model is a much better choice than a general-purpose language model. This is particularly good news for applications where privacy matters and you don't want to send potentially sensitive information to an external server.

For a small collection of documents, this approach is definitely worth testing. Of course, for larger datasets you'd need to think about indexing, storage, and performance. In my demo, the embeddings are kept in memory, which is perfectly sufficient for the example. But the basic idea works surprisingly well.

5. Pause & Ask

Okay, this one might be a little less practical, but it's definitely fancy! 😀 And I think it also has interesting accessibility potential. For this demo, I'm using LFM2.5-VL-450M, a vision-language model with approximately 450 million parameters. The download is roughly 350–400 MB, depending on the configuration.

There are actually two features here. The first is live visual description. I turn on my webcam, and the model periodically describes what it sees. Yes, that's me:

But then it gets even better! I can pause the camera on a particular frame and ask the model questions about what it sees.

And here's the example showing that the model isn't exactly perfect. 😅 Although, well, I'm certainly flattered!

I wouldn't treat this as a reliable accessibility tool just yet, but as an experiment in local visual question answering, it's genuinely fascinating.

And that's all five demos!

So What's the Catch?

Now, as promised, let's talk about the disadvantages. Because, of course, there are quite a few!

WebGPU Support and Hardware Limitations

First of all, these models run as well as they do largely thanks to WebGPU. This API allows applications to use GPU computing capabilities directly in the browser, which can make a huge difference for machine learning inference.

The problem is that WebGPU availability and performance aren't the same on every device. Support has improved significantly across modern browsers, but availability still depends on the browser version, operating system, GPU, drivers, etc. And even if WebGPU is supported, that doesn't mean everyone has an equally powerful computer.

Mobile devices are a particularly interesting problem. Some mobile browsers and devices still lack usable WebGPU support for certain workloads. In those cases, some Transformers.js models can fall back to WebAssembly-based CPU inference, potentially using SIMD or multithreading depending on the environment and configuration.

Unfortunately, this can be significantly slower. On my phone, two of the examples from my demo didn't work at all because they timed out. And it's not like I'm using some ancient phone from a museum! It's a Samsung Galaxy S24 FE. Not the newest flagship anymore, but definitely not a dinosaur either.

So yes, WebGPU support is improving, and the models are getting better. But I want to talk about what we can actually use right now, not what might be possible in a few years.

Model Downloads Aren't Exactly Tiny

There's also another important limitation: the models themselves have to be downloaded. And while some are relatively small, others can require hundreds of megabytes. As you've seen, the models in my demo range from around 23 MB for the quantized semantic search model to nearly 800 MB for the Smart Ticket Creator. That's quite a lot if you're visiting a website on a mobile connection!

Fortunately, browsers can cache the downloaded model files, so subsequent visits usually don't require downloading everything again. But the first load still matters, and browser storage isn't guaranteed to keep those files forever.

That's another reason why I'd treat these features as optional enhancements rather than something every user must load before they can use the application.

Some Things Still Don't Work Well Enough

I also couldn't implement everything I originally wanted, even though some ideas seemed perfectly reasonable. For example, I tried adding text recognition from images. And despite experimenting with different models and configurations, I couldn't get results that were reliable enough for my demo. The approaches I tested didn't give me the quality I wanted, so I decided not to include that feature.

Another thing I wanted to improve was the contextual information in the alt text generator. Imagine uploading a photo of a dog and adding some additional context, such as: "This dog is available for adoption at a local animal shelter." Ideally, the model would take that information into account and generate a beautiful, context-aware description.

I tried using an additional local language model for this, hoping it could combine the visual description with the extra information. But no matter what I tried, the results were very unsatisfactory. So I ended up with the simpler approach I mentioned earlier, where the context is added separately rather than genuinely interpreted by the image-captioning model.

And that's another good example of why I wouldn't blindly trust these models in production.

What About Voice Recognition?

On the other hand, I've heard that small browser-based models can be surprisingly good at speech recognition. Transformers.js supports audio-related tasks too, so that's definitely another interesting area to explore.

I didn't test it this time, though. Mostly because I was building these demos in the evenings, and my family would have killed me if I'd spent hours talking to my computer. 😂 Maybe next time!

My Verdict: Is Browser AI Production-Ready?

So, to sum up: browser-based AI models are getting better, and I think it's already worth exploring how to use them in production applications.

Not necessarily as a replacement for every AI backend. And definitely not as a critical dependency without a fallback. But as optional features that improve the user experience? Absolutely.

What do you think? Have you already experimented with running AI models directly in the browser?

And if you enjoy reading my articles, feel free to follow me on LinkedIn too! 🙂

articles.title: Integrating SEO Components into Discord
articles.description: If you paste a link to your website in a Discord channel, a small card appears automatically: title,...
articles.body_html:
If you paste a link to your website in a Discord channel, a small card appears automatically: title, description, and an image. You didn’t have to write any special code for this, it’s the default behavior.

Discord has just added another option: to completely replace this card with a custom preview, featuring formatted text, an image gallery, and buttons.

I tested this on this blog, and here's how it works.

Here's what you need to have set up before you start:

  • A site served over HTTPS
  • Open Graph tags already present (required, even with an embed component)
  • Server-side rendering (the HTML must contain the tags in the response itself, not after a JavaScript script)
  • The Discordbot crawler is allowed if a WAF, CDN, or rate limiter is in front of the site
  • The embed component's JSON payload is ready (we'll get to that next)

Default Behavior: Open Graph Tags

Without going into further detail, here's what happens: Discord sends a request to your URL, reads the HTML returned by the server, and looks for Open Graph tags in the <head> element.

If they're there, a card is automatically generated.

<meta property="og:title" content="Title of this page" />
<meta property="og:description" content="Description of this page" />
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/og-image.png" />
<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/page" />
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image" />

How it appears on Discord, based solely on these tags:

Here are three key points about how this works, because they’re important for what comes next as well:

  • The tags must be in the HTML sent by the server. Discord does not execute any JavaScript; a tag added later by client-side JS does not exist for Discord.
  • The crawler identifies itself with the user-agent Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Discordbot/2.0; +https://discordapp.com). If a WAF or rate limiter blocks bots, you must explicitly allow Discordbot through.
  • The preview is cached for about 30 minutes. To force a refresh during testing, simply add ?v=2 to the URL.

I go into detail about these Open Graph tags (image sizes, Twitter Card tags, etc.) in "A Few Tips for Improving Your SEO" if you want to explore that topic further.

The new format: component embeds

If there are no embed components on the page, Discord displays nothing more than the card shown above.

This is an addition, not a mandatory replacement: the og:* tags are still required in all cases. They serve as a fallback if the embed cannot be displayed (e.g., a context that doesn’t support it, an invalid payload, etc.).

On the crawler side, the process is the same as for the standard card, with one additional step:

  1. A link to your page is posted in a Discord message.
  2. Discord fetches the URL and reads the HTML.
  3. It also looks for an embed component tag. If it exists, it parses the JSON and retrieves the metadata for each image in the payload.
  4. If the payload is valid, it replaces the Open Graph card with this custom rendering. Otherwise, it goes back to the previous step.

Two ways to display this JSON:

Option 1, inline, a <script> within the <head>:

<script id="discord:component-embed" type="application/json">
  {
    "component": {
      "type": 17,
      "components": [
        {
          "type": 10,
          "content": "# Patch Notes\n- Correction d'un bug d'affichage"
        }
      ]
    }
  }
</script>

Option 2, in external JSON, with a link pointing to a file on the same domain (or a subdomain):

<link
  rel="discord:component-embed"
  type="application/json"
  href="https://exemple.com/embeds/article.json"
/>

This option has a strict limit: 3,000 bytes for the raw file. For an embed with an image gallery and buttons, the inline option allows for a larger size.

The root component must be a *Container (type: 17).

It can contain up to 40 components in total, from among those listed in the table below. Any other component type invalidates the entire payload:

Type Component Notes
1 Action Row row of buttons
2 Button link style only (style: 5), with label and/or emoji
9 Section text + an element (thumbnail or button)
10 Text Display Discord Markdown (headings, bold, lists, links...)
11 Thumbnail small image attached to a Section
12 Media Gallery up to several images/videos, in large format
14 Separator separator line
17 Container the root component

For images (thumbnails and Media Gallery), you only need to provide the URL; Discord will automatically retrieve the dimensions and file type:

{ “url”: “https://exemple.com/images/hero.webp” }

Supported formats: PNG, GIF, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, and for the Media Gallery, MP4/MOV/WebM as well.

What I've set up on my blog

On every post on my blog, in addition to the standard Open Graph tags (which are still there, hidden), I now include an embed component.

It’s built using the same data as the standard card: the title, description, cover image, and the post’s accent color.

The structure looks like this, simplified:

{
  "component": {
    "type": 17,
    "accent_color": 5793266,
    "components": [
      {
        "type": 10,
        "content": "# [Title of the post](https://thomasbnt.dev/blog/...)\nDescription."
      },
      {
        "type": 12,
        "items": [{ "media": { "url": "https://thomasbnt.dev/.../index.png" } }]
      },
      {
        "type": 1,
        "components": [
          {
            "type": 2,
            "style": 5,
            "url": "https://thomasbnt.dev/blog/...",
            "label": "Lire l'article"
          },
          {
            "type": 2,
            "style": 5,
            "url": "https://thomasbnt.dev/blog/",
            "label": "Blog"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The final result on Discord:

Some decisions made while building it:

  • Media Gallery instead of Thumbnail: At first, I went with a Section + Thumbnail, but the image looked tiny next to the text. The Media Gallery displays the image in full size, like a real banner.
  • No Separator: It visually broke up the embed for no reason between the text and the image.
  • Two buttons: one to read the article, one to return to the blog. Simple, but it provides an additional entry point directly from Discord.
  • accent_color: this is an integer, not a hexadecimal color. This blog already has a color associated with each article (backgroundColor in the frontmatter). I simply convert it to decimal (parseInt(hex.replace(“#”, “”), 16)) rather than managing a new one.

As with the OG tags, this script is generated on the server side during the build (the site is built with Astro, so everything is static), so there’s nothing to execute on the client side.

Common issues to avoid

  • A component not on the list, or an extra key on a button (id, custom_id...) invalidates the entire payload, not just the offending component.
  • Removing OG tags because you think they’re no longer needed. They’re still essential: they serve as a fallback whenever the embed doesn’t display.
  • The 30-minute cache. While testing, adding ?v=2 to the URL saves you from wondering for ten minutes why nothing is changing.
  • The 10-second time limit. The entire fetch, including images, must be completed within this timeframe. With a Media Gallery that loads multiple images, this limit is reached faster than with a simple og:image.

How to Test

Discord Embed Debugger shows exactly how the crawler reads a URL: which tags it found, and which embed format it chose. This should be your first step before looking for a bug elsewhere.

Conclusion

To summarize the logic: even without taking any action, Discord already displays a card based on the og:* tags.

Adding an embed component is an additional option, not a replacement. It only activates if the JSON payload is present and valid; otherwise, Discord automatically falls back to the default card.

On this blog, it’s a simple change: same title, same description, same image as the standard card, just presented differently with direct access to the rest of the blog.

Resources

  • Official documentation on component embeds: the complete spec, with all component types and their constraints.
  • Embed Debugger: to see exactly how Discord reads a given URL.
  • Some tips for improving your SEO: Open Graph tags, Core Web Vitals, and other technical basics.
  • This blog’s Discord server: to test your links or discuss all of this.

articles.body_html:
Intro

AI Avatar is a free app where your VRoid (VRM) avatar cheers you with all its might.🤗 It lives in your VS Code sidebar (reacts to Claude Code /Codex /GitHub Copilot) or browser side panel (reacts to ChatGPT / Claude). Animations and speech bubbles all run without AI too.
This time, I have 5 main topics.

  • Avatar Run
  • Muscle Brain 2D/3D
  • Voxel Vatatar Update
  • Jev
  • Codex Support

Let's check them out together!😆

Avatar Run


Avatar Run is a marble-run-type game where you avoid traps, try not to fall off the track, and reach the goal. First, I added a marble run to make AI Avatar more fun. But wait, I wanted to make it match the AI Avatar world better and change the marble to an avatar. Now an avatar runs around the track instead of a marble. But I also added a button so you can enjoy the marble version too. Maybe I will add an auto mode so you can enjoy Avatar Run while coding, like Voxel Avatar, in the future.

Muscle Brain 2D/3D


I made a brain training game called Muscle Brain last year and released it on the Microsoft Store and as a Chrome extension. I completely forgot about it for a long time, but recently I checked its status and found that it was still getting downloads. So I decided to migrate it to AI Avatar.

It was made with Next.js, React, KendoReact, and CSS-in-JS + Tailwind CSS, but AI Avatar was mostly made with plain TypeScript, so I had to rewrite the code. I thought it would be easy for AI to do this. However, the output had many regressions. I asked AI to fix them several times, but there were still many regressions. Then I noticed that the total code length was only half that of the original.🤣 That was why fixing the regressions never ended. So I gave up and started the migration from the beginning. This time, I strongly instructed AI not to cut any code and finally succeeded in the migration.

Also, the original Muscle Brain was a brain training game for remembering numbers or letters. So I added a new version for remembering 3D spatial information and created the new Muscle Brain 3D.

Voxel Avatar Update

v22↓

v21↓

Voxel Avatar is an idle game where you can grow a garden and place animals. You can grow the garden automatically or manually.

This time, I added more gardening patterns, animals, and user experience improvements like an outline display setting. I also added a roller coaster builder so you can take a ride and look around the voxel world.

Creating 3D Models with AI

I wanted to make 3D object models with AI before and add them to AI Avatar. However, AI was not good at handling 3D, so I put the idea on hold. But at last, AI caught up, so I tried to make 3D objects using AI.

First, I made an image using ChatGPT. The point is to make not only a front view but also side and top views.

Next, I made my AI write Three.js code to display a 3D object. I made a harness to repeatedly generate Three.js 3D object code, compare the result with the reference image, and fix the code to get closer to the reference image. This way, I could run the AI autonomously for a while.

After I made the harness, I thought I no longer needed to use the latest, most expensive AI, Astra. So I tried it with the more affordable AI model Sonnet 5 to cut costs. However, it couldn't make a 3D model at all. 🤣

I think making 3D models depends on the AI model, not my harness. But the latest Opus 5.5 and Sol 6.1 have been released, so the situation might change if I test them again.

Jev


Jev is a new AI that has features such as running super fast and being super cheap. This is possible because it does not use text but responds only with decisions and their scores.

I already had a positive/negative checker and feedback animations in AI Avatar. It was just determining positive/negative sentiment using a word list, and its accuracy was not good. So I updated it using Jev's ability to determine positive/negative sentiment.

Also, I added a dev log that can record Claude Code / Codex requests like bug fixes, new features, questions, and others, and display them by day, week, or all time. I hope this log will motivate developers to code more.

Codex Support

I am using both Claude Code and Codex at work. However, I was only using Claude Code at home. This time, I wanted to use Astra because I heard it was good at handling 3D and thought it would be good for adding new 3D objects to Voxel Avatar in AI Avatar. So I subscribed to Codex and also decided to make AI Avatar react to Codex.

How to Use the AI Avatar VS Code Extension Version (Thank you 300+ installs!)

You can download the AI Avatar VS Code extension in two ways.

  • Option 1: Install from VS Code: Extensions button in the left sidebar > Search AI Avatar > Install ↓↓

  • Option 2: Install from the VS Code Marketplace: https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=web-developer-hyper.ai-avatar ↓↓

How to Use the AI Avatar Chrome Version

Install from Chrome Web Store: ↓↓
https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/ai-avatar/afmcfaeaaojalninahhhjnonhmlmiidi

Special Thanks

  • My DEV Community friend and CCO (Chief Creative Officer) 🤣, @annavi11arrea1 collaborated with Catbot and AI Avatar in version 17, and keeps supporting me. Thank you very much!
  • My friend and CDO (Chief Design Officer)🤣, @rutenveil helped create the cool effects in version 15. and keeps supporting me. Thank you very much!
  • My DEV Community friend and CTO (Chief Technology Officer)🤣, @gramli helped update AI Avatar in version 2, and keeps supporting me. Thank you very much!
  • My DEV Community friend and CMO (Chief Marketing Officer)🤣, @itsugo. Our avatar collaboration project was the beginning of AI Avatar, and keeps supporting me. Thank you very much!
  • My colleague Maximum Blue helped make unique avatars in version, 6 and keeps supporting me. Thank you very much!

Version 26 Update

I'm already working on the version 26 update. More fun updates, so please stay tuned!

Outro

Ah! It's time to go for a run with my avatar, so I have to go now.💨 I would love to add more fun features and also use the latest AI in my next updates. I hope you enjoy the new updates to AI Avatar. Thank you for reading, and have a wonderful AI Avatar life!

Comments Welcome!

  • Do you have any ideas to make AI Avatar even more fun?
  • Do you have any ideas to add more AI features?
  • Do you have any ideas for making cool avatars and animations?
  • Do you have any ideas to improve the user experience?
  • Do you have any ideas for increasing the number of users of AI Avatar?

Any other comments are also welcome!

articles.title: How Do You Validate `unknown` in TypeScript Without a Schema Library? 🛡️
articles.description: Hoi hoi! 👋  I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who is obsessed with gamba. 😸🦐  Recently, I was...
articles.body_html:
Hoi hoi! 👋

I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who is obsessed with gamba. 😸🦐

Recently, I was thinking about a very common TypeScript problem.

Suppose some value comes from:

  • an API response
  • JSON.parse
  • local storage
  • a message payload
  • third-party code

What type should it have before we actually verify it?

Probably this

declare const input: unknown;

That part is easy.

The interesting question is what comes next.

How do we safely turn that unknown into something useful?

And do we really need a full schema library every time?

Let's look at it! 👀

Validate unknown in TypeScript Without a Schema Library | is-kit

Validate unknown TypeScript values with small composable type guards and safeParse, without adopting a schema-first validation workflow.

is-kit.dev

🧱 unknown Is Doing Its Job

Suppose we have

declare const input: unknown;

input.name;
// Error

TypeScript refuses to let us access name.

At first this can feel annoying.

But TypeScript is actually telling us something important

We have a value.

We do not know what it is yet.

That is exactly what an untrusted boundary value should mean.

An HTTP response does not become a User just because our application expects a User.

Neither does parsed JSON.

So I like to think of unknown like this

unknown is not missing type information.

It is an honest description of a value we have not verified yet.

The problem is not unknown.

The problem is how we establish trust.

😈 The Easy Escape: as User

There is a very short way out.

type User = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
};

declare const input: unknown;

const user = input as User;

user.name.toUpperCase();

TypeScript is happy.

Nice! 🎉

Except, nothing was actually checked.

This still works

const input = {
  id: "user-1",
  name: 123,
} as unknown;

const user = input as User;

user.name.toUpperCase();
// 💥 Runtime error

as User changes what the compiler believes.

It does not inspect the runtime value.
It does not add missing properties.
It does not turn 123 into a string.

So if runtime trust matters, a type assertion is not validation.

We need an actual runtime check.

🛡️ A Type Guard Connects Runtime and TypeScript

Let's start small.

With is-kit, we can build a guard like this

import { isString, oneOfValues, struct } from "is-kit";

const isUser = struct({
  id: isString,
  name: isString,
  role: oneOfValues("admin", "member"),
});

Now we can pass unknown directly to it

declare const input: unknown;

if (isUser(input)) {
  input.name.toUpperCase();

  // input:
  // Readonly<{
  //   id: string;
  //   name: string;
  //   role: "admin" | "member";
  // }>
}

This is the part I like.

The same check does two jobs

runtime
→ does this value actually match?

TypeScript
→ what is this value after the check succeeds?

There is no separate schema definition and no type assertion.

We just compose small runtime predicates.

🧩 The Shape Can Grow Naturally

Real payloads are usually a little more complicated.

Maybe a user has:

  • an optional profile
  • a nullable bio
  • a list of tags

We can keep composing guards

import {
  arrayOf,
  isString,
  nullable,
  oneOfValues,
  optionalKey,
  struct,
} from "is-kit";

const isProfile = struct({
  displayName: isString,
  bio: optionalKey(nullable(isString)),
});

const isUser = struct({
  id: isString,
  role: oneOfValues("admin", "member"),
  profile: optionalKey(isProfile),
  tags: arrayOf(isString),
});

Then

isUser({
  id: "user-1",
  role: "member",
  tags: ["typescript", "guards"],
});
// true

But

isUser({
  id: "user-1",
  role: "owner",
  tags: ["typescript"],
});
// false

Each piece is still just a guard.

That means we can test it independently, reuse it somewhere else, or compose it into something larger.

There is also an important difference here

optionalKey(...)

means

the property may be absent

while

nullable(...)

means

the value may be null

Those are different runtime contracts, so I prefer keeping them separate.

📦 What Does safeParse Add?

A direct guard is often enough.

if (isUser(input)) {
  renderUser(input);
}

But sometimes I want the validation result itself to move through the program.

For example

const result = safeParse(isUser, input);

if (!result.valid) {
  return { status: 400 as const };
}

return {
  status: 200 as const,
  user: result.value,
};

safeParse gives us a small tagged result

{
  valid: (true, value);
}

or

{
  valid: false;
}

So TypeScript can narrow it with a normal branch.

The important part is what safeParse does not do.

It does not:

  • clone the value
  • coerce the value
  • generate a new object
  • transform invalid data into valid data

On success, it returns the same value after the guard has accepted it.

So I think of the difference like this

guard
→ boolean + narrowing

safeParse
→ tagged result + validated value

Same runtime rule.

Different control-flow shape.

🧃 What About JSON?

This is one of the most common boundaries.

const value = JSON.parse(body);

The awkward part is that JSON.parse returns any.

So now the unsafe value can spread through the program before we validate it.

Instead, we can keep the boundary small

import { safeJsonParse } from "is-kit";

declare const body: string;

const result = safeJsonParse(body, isUser);

if (!result.valid) {
  return { status: 400 as const };
}

renderUser(result.value);

Conceptually, the flow is

JSON text
   ↓
decode
   ↓
unknown
   ↓
guard
   ↓
validated value

Invalid JSON and guard failures both produce

{
  valid: false;
}

And again, nothing is coerced just to make the value pass.

I like this because the unsafe part stays right at the decode boundary.

🚪 Should Extra Keys Be Allowed?

There is another small design choice that appears at object boundaries.

Suppose we expect

{
  username: string;
  password: string;
}

Should this also be accepted?

{
  username: "Neko",
  password: "secret",
  admin: true,
}

With struct, extra keys are allowed by default.

That is often useful for API responses because a server may add a new field without breaking an older client.

But sometimes we really want a closed object shape.

Then we can use

const isCredentials = struct(
  {
    username: isString,
    password: isString,
  },
  { exact: true },
);

Now

isCredentials({
  username: "Neko",
  password: "secret",
});
// true

while

isCredentials({
  username: "Neko",
  password: "secret",
  admin: true,
});
// false

The important part is not that one mode is always better.

It is that the boundary should express the contract we actually want.

🤔 So Do We Still Need Schema Libraries?

Yes.

Sometimes absolutely.

A type guard toolkit and a schema library overlap a little, but they are not trying to solve exactly the same problem.

For example, a schema library is probably the better choice when we need:

  • structured validation errors with field paths
  • multiple validation issues at once
  • coercion
  • default values
  • transformations
  • schema-generated types or external artifacts
  • deep integration with a form or API framework

Those are larger validation workflows.

is-kit asks a narrower question

Does this value satisfy this runtime predicate?

If yes, what can TypeScript safely narrow it to?

That narrower model is sometimes exactly what I want.

For example

Approach Good fit
Inline typeof checks One small local condition
Type guards Reusable boolean validation and narrowing
Schema library Rich validation, transformation, and schema workflows

So I don't think the question is

Type guards or schema libraries—which one wins?

The more useful question is

What is the smallest validation model that solves this boundary?

🎯 The Important Part

I started with a simple value

declare const input: unknown;

The tempting shortcut was

const user = input as User;

But that only changes TypeScript's belief.

It does not establish runtime trust.

A runtime guard gives us a much more useful flow

unknown
   ↓
runtime check
   ↓
narrowed value

And when we want a result-oriented API

unknown
   ↓
guard
   ↓
safeParse
   ↓
{ valid: true, value }
or
{ valid: false }

No hidden conversion.

No assertion pretending the check already happened.

Just small runtime rules that TypeScript can understand too. 😸

If you want to see the full guide, including JSON boundaries, exact objects, and custom domain refinements:

Validate unknown in TypeScript Without a Schema Library | is-kit

Validate unknown TypeScript values with small composable type guards and safeParse, without adopting a schema-first validation workflow.

is-kit.dev

And if you want to explore is-kit itself:

nyaomaru / is-kit

Build small guards. Compose them. A lightweight, zero-dependency toolkit for building reusable TypeScript type guards that compose, refine, and preserve natural narrowing. Runtime-safe 🛡️, composable 🧩, and ergonomic ✨.

Build small guards. Compose them.

is-kit is a lightweight, zero-dependency toolkit for building reusable TypeScript type guards.

is-kit is not just a collection of isX helpers. Its main focus is composing small runtime checks into reusable guards while preserving useful TypeScript narrowing.

It helps you write small isFoo functions, compose them into richer runtime checks, refine properties on values you already know about, and keep TypeScript narrowing natural inside regular control flow. Use it at runtime boundaries when needed, without requiring a schema-first workflow.

Runtime-safe 🛡️, composable 🧩, and ergonomic ✨ without asking you to adopt a heavy schema workflow.

  • Build and reuse typed guards
  • Compose guards with and, or, not, oneOf
  • Use refineKey to narrow a child property while preserving its parent type
  • Validate object shapes and collections when that is useful

articles.title: Zone.js Hijacked Your Browser for 8 Years. Here's What Replaced It.
articles.description: A visual deep dive into how Angular tore out global browser monkey-patching and rebuilt its reactivity engine from scratch using Signals and Zoneless change detection.
articles.body_html:
Every frontend framework has to solve the same foundational challenge: when data changes in memory, how does the framework know which pixels on the screen need updating?

React chose virtual DOM diffing. Svelte chose compile-time DOM mutations.

For nearly ten years, Angular had the strangest answer in modern web development: it hijacked your entire browser.

If you called setTimeout, Angular intercepted it. If you clicked a button, Angular hijacked addEventListener. If you fetched data over the network, Angular wrapped fetch and XMLHttpRequest.

The library doing this heavy lifting was called Zone.js. It did not actually know what data changed, or which component owned that data. It only knew one blunt fact: an asynchronous browser API had finished running.

Because something might have changed, Angular did the only thing it could: it walked down your entire component tree, checking every single binding from top to bottom.

Over the last few versions, the Angular team quietly pulled off one of the most audacious architectural rewiring jobs in frontend history. They removed the monkey-patches, dismantled the global tree scans, and rebuilt Angular around Signals and Zoneless change detection.

To write modern, high-performance Angular, you have to understand how the old trick worked, why it ran out of road, and how the new reactive engine actually updates your DOM today.

The Zone.js Era: The Illusion of Automatic Reactivity

To understand where Angular is today, we have to look at what Zone.js was actually doing behind the scenes.

Consider this classic Angular component:

@Component({
  selector: 'app-counter',
  template: `
    <button (click)="increment()">Clicks: {{ count }}</button>
  `
})
export class CounterComponent {
  count = 0;

  increment() {
    this.count++;
  }
}

Notice what is missing here:

  • No setState() call like in React.
  • No this.triggerUpdate() call.
  • Just a plain property mutation: this.count++.

How did Angular know that this.count changed from 0 to 1?

The surprising answer is: it didn't.

Angular had no idea that count was touched. Instead, when your application booted up, Zone.js replaced the browser's native addEventListener with a patched wrapper.

When the user clicked the button, the execution pipeline went like this:

  1. The browser fired the native click event.
  2. Zone.js intercepted the callback.
  3. Your increment() function ran and mutated this.count.
  4. Zone.js detected that the microtask queue was empty (onMicrotaskEmpty).
  5. Zone.js notified Angular: "An async task just completed."
  6. Angular executed ApplicationRef.tick().
  7. Angular started at the very top of your application (the Root Component) and traversed every active child component, evaluating every template expression to see if any value differed from the previous cycle. 
       User Action (Click / Timer / Network Fetch)
                           │
                           ▼
          Browser Native API Intercepted by Zone.js
                           │
                           ▼
              Component Handler Executes
              (count++ in component memory)
                           │
                           ▼
          Zone.js Microtask Queue Becomes Empty
                           │
                           ▼
              Notify Angular: onMicrotaskEmpty
                           │
                           ▼
               ApplicationRef.tick()
                           │
        ┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐
        ▼                                     ▼
   Root Component                     Component Tree Walk
   (Check bindings)                 (Check every child node)

This model was convenient, but it was an architectural blunt instrument.

If you had a dashboard with 2,000 components and a setInterval ticking in a background widget, Angular could end up checking thousands of template expressions every second, even if 99% of those components were completely static.

Why OnPush Was Only a Partial Cure

To stop these wasteful global tree traversals, Angular introduced ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush.

When you marked a component as OnPush, you gave Angular permission to skip that component's subtree during a change detection cycle, unless one of a few specific conditions was met:

  1. One of the component's @Input() references changed to a new memory address.
  2. An event listener declared directly inside that component's template was triggered.
  3. An AsyncPipe in the template emitted a new value.
  4. You manually injected ChangeDetectorRef and called markForCheck().

OnPush delivered enormous performance boosts, but it shifted mental overhead onto the developer. Mutating an object property in place broke change detection because the object reference remained unchanged.

Developers spent years debugging "ghost states", situations where component properties held fresh data, but the screen refused to re-render because no input reference had swapped.

The New Foundation: Signals and the Dependency Graph

Modern Angular replaces the global guessing game with a fine-grained reactive dependency graph powered by Signals.

A Signal is not an event stream, and it is not an RxJS Subject. A Signal is a synchronous reactive value wrapper that implements a two-way contract between Producers and Consumers.

import { signal, computed } from '@angular/core';

// Producer: holds a value and tracks who is listening
const count = signal(0);
const multiplier = signal(2);

// Producer & Consumer: listens to dependencies, produces a new value
const total = computed(() => count() * multiplier());

Here is what happens inside the runtime when this code runs:

  1. When computed() evaluates its formula, it temporarily registers itself as the active consumer on the global execution stack.
  2. Calling count() reads the current number, but it also registers an invisible edge in the dependency graph: total depends on count.
  3. Calling multiplier() registers another edge: total depends on multiplier.
  4. The graph is now wired.

When you update a signal via count.set(5), Angular does not re-run every calculation immediately.

Instead, it uses a push-pull algorithm:

  • Push notification: The changed signal pushes a lightweight "dirty" flag down the dependency graph to all consumers.
  • Pull evaluation: The consumer only recalculates its value when someone actually reads it.

If a computed signal is never read by an active template, it does not do the calculation work. This guarantees that your application never spends CPU cycles computing state that nobody is looking at.

Going Zoneless: How Angular Knows to Refresh the Screen

With Signals in place, modern Angular takes the decisive next step: eliminating Zone.js entirely.

You can configure an Angular application to run in Zoneless mode with a single provider:

// app.config.ts
import { ApplicationConfig, provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection } from '@angular/core';

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()
  ]
};

When you turn off Zone.js, the monkey-patches disappear. Angular stops intercepting setTimeout, fetch, and native DOM events.

Without Zone.js waking up Angular, how does the framework know when to update the DOM?

Modern Angular introduces the ChangeDetectionScheduler. Instead of listening to global browser events, the scheduler only wakes up when it receives an explicit notification from one of five distinct sources:

  1. A Signal read in a template updates its value: When a template reads {{ user() }}, the template's view becomes a reactive consumer. Calling user.set(newProfile) flags that view dirty.
  2. A template event listener fires: When a user clicks <button (click)="save()">, Angular's template binding triggers the scheduler.
  3. An AsyncPipe emits: The pipe explicitly schedules a render check when new data arrives.
  4. An input changes: Calling ComponentRef.setInput() notifies the scheduler.
  5. Manual notification: An explicit call to ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck().

When any of these triggers fire, the ChangeDetectionScheduler batches the requests into a single microtask using the browser's native queueMicrotask.

Even if your code updates fifty signals across three services in the same synchronous execution block, Angular only runs change detection once on the next microtask tick.

And when it runs, it checks only the components and views that were marked dirty by the reactive graph. Unaffected parts of the tree are completely skipped.

Seeing the Difference: A Real Code Walkthrough

Let us look at how this changes everyday component code.

Here is a modern, Zoneless-ready Angular component:

import { Component, signal, computed } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-order-summary',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <div class="card">
      <h2>Order Total: ${{ total() }}</h2>
      <p>Items in cart: {{ itemCount() }}</p>

      <button (click)="addItem(25)">Add $25 Item</button>
      <button (click)="clearCart()">Reset</button>
    </div>
  `
})
export class OrderSummaryComponent {
  // Writable Signals
  private prices = signal<number[]>([10, 20]);

  // Derived Computed Signal
  itemCount = computed(() => this.prices().length);
  total = computed(() => this.prices().reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0));

  addItem(price: number) {
    this.prices.update(items => [...items, price]);
  }

  clearCart() {
    this.prices.set([]);
  }
}

What makes this component fundamentally different from older Angular versions?

First, there are no lifecycle hacks. You do not need ngOnChanges or manual subscriptions to calculate derived totals. If prices changes, total and itemCount update their dependencies automatically.

Second, in a Zoneless setup, clicking the button does not trigger a global audit of other unrelated components across your app.

The update to prices marks the template view of OrderSummaryComponent as dirty. The scheduler coalesces the update, visits this single component during the microtask, and patches the two interpolation text nodes directly.

Three Traps to Avoid When Moving to Zoneless

As teams migrate their codebases toward Zoneless Angular, three common pitfalls tend to surface:

Trap 1: Mutating Plain Class Properties

In the old Zone.js world, this code worked because Zone.js caught the click event and checked everything anyway:

// ❌ Old habit that breaks in Zoneless
export class ProfileComponent {
  userName = 'Sarah';

  updateName() {
    this.userName = 'Alex'; // Screen will NOT update if triggered outside template events!
  }
}

If updateName() is called from a WebSocket event, an RxJS stream, or a native callback, Angular has no way of knowing this.userName changed.

The Fix: Wrap mutable view state in a Signal:

// ✅ Zoneless-safe
export class ProfileComponent {
  userName = signal('Sarah');

  updateName() {
    this.userName.set('Alex');
  }
}

Trap 2: Unintended Signal Tracking Inside Effects

Angular provides effect() for running side effects when signals change (such as logging or syncing to local storage).

effect(() => {
  console.log(`Current user: ${this.currentUser()}`);
  // If you also read another signal here for logging...
  console.log(`Analytics ID: ${this.analyticsId()}`);
});

Because effect() tracks every signal read within its callback, this effect will re-run whenever currentUser changes, but also whenever analyticsId changes.

The Fix: Use untracked() when you only want to read a secondary signal without subscribing to it:

import { effect, untracked } from '@angular/core';

effect(() => {
  const user = this.currentUser();
  const id = untracked(() => this.analyticsId());

  console.log(`User ${user} logged with ID ${id}`);
});

Trap 3: Subscribing to Observables Without AsyncPipe or toSignal

If your service returns an RxJS Observable and you subscribe manually without updating a Signal or calling markForCheck(), your Zoneless view will stay silent:

// ❌ Manual subscription without notification
this.dataService.fetch().subscribe(data => {
  this.rawData = data; // UI does not refresh in Zoneless mode
});

The Fix: Convert the Observable directly into a Signal using toSignal():

import { toSignal } from '@angular/core/rxjs-interop';

// ✅ Seamlessly bridges RxJS and Angular's reactive graph
readonly data = toSignal(this.dataService.fetch(), { initialValue: [] });

The Paradigm Shift at a Glance

Feature The Zone.js Era Modern Zoneless Angular
Change Detection Trigger Global browser monkey-patching Explicit Signal / Event notifications
Checking Scope Top-down tree traversal by default Targeted dirty views only
Async API Handling Intercepts setTimeout, Promise, fetch Leaves browser APIs untouched
Reactive Primitive RxJS Observables / plain variables Fine-grained Signals (signal, computed)
Derived State Getters or manual subscriptions computed() with push-pull caching
Bundle Overhead Carried zone.js runtime (~35-40 kB) Zero Zone.js runtime overhead
Debugging Stack Traces Polluted with internal Zone frames Clean, native JavaScript stack traces

The Clean Framework Angular Always Wanted to Be

When Angular 2 launched, Zone.js felt like pure magic. You wrote plain TypeScript, touched a variable, and the screen updated without any explicit ceremony.

Yet that magic came at a steep cost: heavy runtime patching, unpredictable global change detection cycles, and cluttered stack traces that made debugging frustrating for newcomers and veterans alike.

By embracing Signals and Zoneless architecture, Angular did not just chase a modern trend. It solved its oldest architectural compromise.

The framework no longer has to guess what your application is doing. Instead, it relies on a clear, mathematically sound dependency graph that knows exactly which data connects to which pixel.

If you have worked with both older Angular and the latest Signal-driven releases, how has the transition changed the way you think about state architecture? And what was the biggest hurdle your team faced when letting go of Zone.js?

References:

  • Angular Official Documentation: Signals
  • Angular Official Documentation: Zoneless Change Detection
  • Angular RFC: Reactivity with Signals
  • Reactivity in Modern Web Frameworks: Push-Pull Algorithms
