articles.description: This is part of my series "My Open-Source Projects", where I walk through the projects I started or...
articles.body_html:
This is part of my series "My Open-Source Projects", where I walk through the projects I started or helped to grow – with the back story, what they do well, where they struggle, and what's next. Previous parts: AngleSharp, MAGES, Piral, Electron.NET and Netpack.

Today's project is the one that is simultaneously my youngest and the one that comes with the biggest "well, actually" disclaimer: Picard.js. It is a micro frontend orchestrator – a small library that can bring micro frontends to any page, no matter how that page was built.

Before you ask: yes, the name is a Star Trek reference. No, I will not stop making "Make it so" jokes. Engage.

What is Picard.js?

Picard.js is a lightweight, flexible variant of the ideas behind Piral. It combines multiple micro frontend technologies – pilets, Module Federation, Native Federation, and more – behind one small, uniform surface. The important bit: you do not need a Piral instance, and you do not need a Native Federation shell, to use it.

The official tagline is "The Captain for Shipping the Next Generation of Micro Frontends Federation and Beyond". The docs also say something I like a lot: Picard is an extension rather than a replacement for the technologies it works with.

In practice that means:

  • You have an existing app – an old PHP site, a static site, an ASP.NET page, a server-rendered thing from 2012 that nobody dares to touch.
  • You add one script tag.
  • You use custom elements such as <pi-component> and <pi-slot> to say where micro frontends should show up.
  • Picard loads them (from whatever format they come in), renders them, and keeps the page alive even if one of them explodes.

That's it. No new build, no new shell, no migration project that needs a steering committee.

How it came to be

If you read the Piral article, you know the deal: Piral is a full framework for micro frontends. App shell, CLI, ecosystem, the works. And very good at it. But a full framework is a full commitment – and not every project can, or wants to, commit.

Over the years the same questions kept coming up:

  • "Can I use this in my existing app without turning it into a Piral app?"
  • "Can I mix pilets with Module Federation?"
  • "Can I just load a micro frontend into a plain HTML page?"

The honest answer was always "sort of, but…". Picard is the "yes" to those questions.

The initial version was outlined at the Micro Frontends Conference in June 2024, where it was revealed in the closing keynote, "Painless Micro Frontend Orchestration with Picard". The pitch back then was: one library to just embed micro frontends – no tooling required, no constraints implied. In your existing web app, in a mobile app, or even in an Electron shell.

The first releases followed quickly in July 2024. And then… things got quiet. Development was paused in 2025 for a while. Life, other projects (hello, Netpack), and the small matter of figuring out what the future of Piral should look like.

That last point is actually the interesting one, because the pause had a purpose.

Picard is the foundation of Piral v2

There is now a clear roadmap for Piral v2, and it is built on top of Picard. The FAQ puts it precisely: Picard is not Piral's successor – it is the base library for Piral v2, effectively replacing piral-base.

So the relationship is:

  • Piral = the full framework (shell, tooling, ecosystem, opinions)
  • Picard = the engine that loads and renders micro frontends (few opinions, many formats)

The most important difference when you pick one: Piral always requires a micro frontend discovery server (a pattern Piral popularized), while Picard treats it as optional. With Picard you can point at a discovery service, hand it a list, give it a function – or simply reference a micro frontend by URL right in the markup.

The Piral v2 plan also gives us a nice tie-in with the Electron.NET article: the presets in the tracking issue are spa, ssr, islands, electron, tauri and react-native. One foundation, many runtimes.

Getting started

The one-liner 

<script src="https://unpkg.com/picard-js"></script>

Drop that into a page (or use jsDelivr, or install it from npm as picard-js) and the custom elements start working. If you have a discovery service, add its URL via the feed attribute on the script tag:

<script src="https://unpkg.com/picard-js" feed="https://feed.example.com/api/v1/pilet"></script>

Rendering a component

The workhorse is <pi-component>. You tell it what to render and where it comes from:

<!-- a Module Federation micro frontend -->
<pi-component
  name="product-teaser"
  source="https://shop.example.com/mf-manifest.json"
  format="module">
</pi-component>

<!-- a Native Federation micro frontend -->
<pi-component
  name="checkout-button"
  source="https://checkout.example.com/remoteEntry.json"
  format="native">
</pi-component>

<!-- a pilet -->
<pi-component
  name="newsletter"
  source="https://cdn.example.com/newsletter/index.meta.json"
  format="pilet">
</pi-component>

Other attributes you will meet along the way include remote-name and remote-type (var or esm) for Module Federation, framework (e.g. single-spa), loading-template-id for a loading placeholder, and client (e.g. visible) to control when it gets activated.

Rendering everything that matches

<pi-slot> is the sibling for the "extension slot" idea you may know from Piral: it renders all components registered under a name – from all loaded micro frontends.

<ul>
  <pi-slot name="menu-item" item-template-id="menu-entry"></pi-slot>
</ul>

<template id="menu-entry">
  <li><slot></slot></li>
</template>

Teams can add menu entries without anyone touching the host page. (Slots also support ordering via attributes.)

Using it from code

Not everything has to be markup. The client variant is a regular module:

import { initializePicard } from 'picard-js/client';

initializePicard({
  feed: 'https://feed.example.com/api/v1/pilet',
});

feed is flexible: a URL string, an array of pilet metadata, a discovery response (Piral Feed Service or the MFE working group schema), a map of Native Federation manifests – or a function returning a promise of any of those.

The generic lifecycle

How does Picard render a component written in React, Vue, Svelte or "something my colleague wrote at 2 am"? Via a small, generic lifecycle:

A component exposes some or all of these. A minimal sketch with React looks like this:

import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { Teaser } from './Teaser';

export default {
  mount(container, props) {
    const root = createRoot(container);
    root.render(<Teaser {...props} />);
    container.__root = root;
  },
  update(container, props) {
    container.__root.render(<Teaser {...props} />);
  },
  unmount(container) {
    container.__root.unmount();
  },
};

If you already have single-spa parcels, there is an adapter for those too (framework="single-spa", client only). So you are not forced to rewrite anything to be "Picard compatible".

Errors stay contained

One thing I care about a lot: a micro frontend that fails to load, or crashes while rendering, must not take the page with it. Picard handles bad references and crashing components gracefully. (For debugging, the Piral Inspector works with Picard, too.)

Server-side rendering and islands

Because Picard is "just" a library with a Node variant, it is not restricted to client-side pages.

  • The node variant (picard-js/node) takes your HTML, finds the pi-component elements, and replaces them with their server-rendered output (via the stringify step of the lifecycle) plus the state the browser needs. There is also the pi-part element – a server-only replacement rule – which, for example, injects the display: contents styling for the custom elements.
  • The islands variant is a lightweight resumption approach: the page already looks right, the interactive script loads after first paint, and components hydrate only where needed (hydrate attribute, or detected in mount by a non-empty container).

The repository's examples cover static pages (with and without a feed, with routing, with single-spa), an SSR example, an islands example, and dependency sharing. And on the server examples we keep a self-imposed rule: they have to reach a Lighthouse score of 100. It's a good constraint to have when your whole purpose is being lightweight.

Where Picard shines

  • Brownfield-friendly. One script tag and some custom elements. Your PHP page doesn't need to know what a bundler is.
  • Format-agnostic. Pilets, Module Federation (v1 and v2), Native Federation and plain native ES modules – side by side, on the same page.
  • Small. The upcoming 0.3.0 reduces the browser script from 106 kB to 33 kB (the Module Federation runtime is loaded on demand), and the interactive script loads after the first paint.
  • Optional discovery. Works great with a discovery server, doesn't require one.
  • Resilient. Broken micro frontends don't break the page.
  • Framework-agnostic. If it can map to the lifecycle, it can be rendered.

Where it struggles (the honest part)

Let's be adults about this:

  • It is an early preview. The changelog says "Early preview: Not suitable for production yet" on every entry. I mean that.
  • The published version is old. The latest release on npm is 0.2.3 from July 2024. The docs already describe 0.3.0, which is still unreleased and lives in develop. (Yes, the docs are ahead of the package. I know.)
  • The docs are thin in places. The Electron page is a placeholder, and the FAQ still has "feature complete by end of July 2024" and "production ready in September 2024". Those dates are… let's call them aspirational. They are on my list for the finalization.
  • Small community. ~49 GitHub stars and a few dozen weekly downloads. Picard is not widely adopted – yet. If you need something battle-tested today, use Piral.
  • Not a framework. There is no CLI that scaffolds your world. That's by design, but it also means more is on you.

Community and licensing

The code is MIT licensed. Questions and discussions happen in the Piral community Discord, and issues and PRs on GitHub are very welcome – especially for the examples and docs.

Contributing is lighter than it sounds: the project uses esbuild for the examples, Playwright for tests (Node 22+), and preview releases (-pre.N) are published straight from develop.

What's next

The roadmap is refreshingly short:

  1. Finalize Picard v1. Settle the API, finish the docs, remove the "early preview" banner. It will ship toward the end of this year (2026).
  2. Piral v2 on top of it, with the presets spa, ssr, islands, electron, tauri and react-native.
  3. More examples and guides – and more FAQ items.

If you have a use case that Picard should handle, please open an issue. This is the right moment to shape it.

Links

  • 🌐 Website: picard.js.org
  • 📖 Docs: picard.js.org/guide
  • 💻 GitHub: picardjs/picard
  • 📦 npm: picard-js

Previous articles in this series:

  • AngleSharp
  • MAGES
  • Piral
  • Electron.NET
  • Netpack

Next up in this series

There are still a few projects waiting in the hangar. Stay tuned – and until then: make it so.

articles.title: Is This How Frontend Developers Work Now? My 2026 Coding Setup
articles.description: Software development is moving fast! The same setup I had six weeks ago, is not the same I have now....
articles.body_html:
Software development is moving fast! The same setup I had six weeks ago, is not the same I have now. In fact, I've been doing software development on my phone!

Just last week I was on vacation at Yellowstone, and I built an app from my phone. I chatted with an agent, it pushed the code to GitHub, and I reviewed the PRs. It was wild!

This post walks through the setup that makes that work. It runs on a server in my house, and I can reach it from anywhere.

Full disclosure, I'm a developer advocate at AWS, and a couple of the tools here are Kiro tools.

The box: a TrueNAS home lab

Years ago I bought an old Intel Xeon server and loaded it with hard drives. It's been my home lab ever since, running TrueNAS. For this setup I created a new Ubuntu VM on it called Kiro Crew and do all my coding there.

I went with Ubuntu 24.04 for the long-term support. 26 was an option, but 24 does everything I need.

You don't need a TrueNAS server for this. I've seen people buy a Mac mini or reuse an old machine, and an EC2 instance or any cloud VM works too. I like keeping it local so everything sits on my own network.

What I installed

After the VM was up, I SSH'd in and installed four things.

  • Kiro CLI. Any coding harness that runs on a remote server and lets you authenticate there will work. Most of them do now.
  • Kiro Crew. This is the agent I actually talk to. It works like a personal assistant for developers, with sessions, artifacts, memories, skills, and scheduled tasks. OpenClaw, Pi, and OpenCode are other options people run on remote servers.
  • The GitHub CLI, so the agent can push code and open PRs.
  • Tailscale, so I can reach the server from anywhere.

Connecting from my phone with Tailscale

Tailscale puts the server, my laptop, and my phone on the same private network. Wherever I am, I open Tailscale on my phone, SSH into the box with a mobile SSH app, and port forward the Kiro Crew dashboard. I use port 5477 for mine.

The Kiro Crew docs cover remote setup, and the remote and mobile guide goes through SSH tunnels and phone access step by step. You could use something like CloudFlare tunnels for this as well.

Connecting from my laptop with SSH port forwarding

From my laptop it's a single SSH command with local port forwarding:

ssh -L 5477:localhost:5477 YOUR_USER@YOUR_SERVER

Then I open a new connection window and point it at that port. (I also installed Kiro Crew locally on my Mac Laptop, so I can connect to Kiro Crew locally or to a remote instance)

For security, Kiro Crew wants a token before it lets you in. On the server, run:

kirocrew token

It prints a link with a token in it. Open that, and you're talking to your Crew instance.

Working in Kiro Crew

Sessions live along the side of the dashboard. When I start a new one, I usually turn on trust mode so the agent stops asking for approval after every step. That isn't a good idea for everything. For the personal projects I'm building, I'm comfortable with it.

Then I tell it what to do. In the video I had it pull down a repo I already had. As we go back and forth, it sends me screenshots of what it's building, and it can spin up a dev server so I can look at the running app.

By default it put that project in a scratch folder. Normally I pick the working folder I want before I start. The artifacts tab collects the screenshots and files from all my other projects too, so I can check on things I'm not actively working on.

Memories and skills

Memories are new in Kiro Crew. I told it to always use Vue.js, because I'm a huge Vue fan. I also installed a set of skills, so every new project starts with the same defaults.

Reviewing stacked PRs on GitHub

I always tell the agent to push to GitHub. When I want to be careful, I ask for a stacked PR.

GitHub's stacked PR interface works well with coding agents. It breaks a large update into smaller layers, and you review each one on its own.

For a fun project I'll accept the whole stack. For anything else I go through it layer by layer, make changes, and go back to Kiro Crew with something like "please update the PR, this code isn't what I want." Then we go back and forth until it's right.

The next thing I'd add is CodeRabbit, which reviews PRs automatically before you merge. I don't have it on this project yet.

Building from my phone on vacation

When I was at Yellowstone National Park last week, I wanted to try an ASCII library I'd seen on Hacker News. I asked Kiro Crew to build an app with it, and it created everything.

I did all of it from my phone. Tailscale got me onto my network, I chatted with the agent, it pushed to GitHub, and I checked the PRs. It worked really well.

I can also give it one prompt, turn on trust mode, walk away, and come back half an hour later to see everything it's done.

Models and effort levels

I switch between Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol. Opus 5.5 works better for me and what I'm building, so that's my default.

I've also been testing different effort levels, including high. I don't have a clear answer there yet, so your mileage may vary.

Specs and parallel sessions

When I want to be very specific, I use spec-driven development mode. Kiro Crew has a spec builder built in. (You can enable it in the "Discover" apps section)

Most of the time, though, I open three or four sessions and let them run in the background while I do other things.

Scheduled tasks and Discord

I'm trying to do more speaking, so I set up a weekly CFP finder. It runs on a schedule and sends me a message with what it found.

Kiro Crew is also connected to my own Discord channel and posts there. So I can either use Tailscale and port forwarding to open Crew on my phone, or I just open Discord and read the messages as they come in.

What does your setup look like?

This is how I'm building apps right now. A server at home runs the agent, my phone and laptop connect to it, and code reaches me as stacked PRs I can review.

Is this what your future looks like? Have you been running agents remotely, or is everything still happening in your editor? Let me know in the comments.

articles.title: 10 Best Jira Integrations for Engineering Teams in 2026
articles.description: Jira is one of the most widely used tools for managing software development projects. Engineering...
articles.body_html:
Jira is one of the most widely used tools for managing software development projects. Engineering teams use it to organize backlogs, plan sprints, track bugs, and coordinate releases.

But managing tickets is only one part of building software.

Developers also work with code repositories, CI/CD pipelines, communication platforms, monitoring tools, and increasingly, AI coding agents. When these tools operate independently, teams can waste time switching between applications, searching for updates, and manually connecting development work to its results.

That's where Jira integrations become useful.

The right integrations can connect issues to code changes, surface build failures, improve team communication, and even help teams experiment with AI agents that execute coding tasks.

In this guide, we'll explore 10 of the best Jira integrations for engineering teams in 2026, what each tool offers, and when it makes sense to use it.

Quick Comparison

Integration capabilities, availability, and pricing depend on your Jira edition and the configuration of each connected product.

1. GitHub — Best for Source Control and Code Reviews

Best for: Engineering teams that use GitHub to host repositories and review code.

GitHub is one of the most useful integrations for teams that use Jira to plan work and GitHub to develop software.

Without an integration, a Jira ticket might say that a bug has been fixed, but developers may still need to open GitHub to locate the relevant branch, commits, and pull request.

Connecting GitHub to Jira brings supported development activity into the context of the Jira work item.

Depending on the configuration, teams can connect:

  • Branches associated with Jira issues
  • Commits referencing issue keys
  • Pull requests and review activity
  • Related build and deployment information

For example, imagine a ticket called PAY-142: Fix payment validation. A developer creates a branch, implements the fix, and opens a pull request referencing PAY-142. The team can then inspect the linked development activity from the corresponding Jira issue.

This improves traceability between requirements and code changes.

Why choose it? GitHub is an excellent starting point if your team wants to reduce manual status updates and make development progress more visible.

Explore: GitHub and Jira integration.

2. GitLab — Best for DevOps Workflows

Best for: Teams using GitLab for source control, merge requests, and CI/CD.

GitLab combines repository management with development automation, making it useful for teams that want to connect Jira planning with their delivery workflow.

Its Jira integration can connect work items to development activity, including commits and merge requests. Teams can also configure supported workflows to coordinate issue tracking with development progress.

For example, a developer working on a new feature can reference a Jira issue in a commit or merge request. This helps the team trace the implementation back to the original requirement.

GitLab is particularly useful when engineering teams already rely on its repositories and CI/CD pipelines.

Why choose it? Choose GitLab if your team wants to retain its existing DevOps environment while making development activity more visible in Jira.

Explore: GitLab's Jira integration documentation.

3. Sharkly — Best for Connecting Jira Work to AI Coding Agents

Best for: Engineering teams that want AI agents to execute coding tasks while keeping their existing Jira workflow connected.

Project management tools help teams decide what needs to be done. Developers then take those tasks into their coding environments, implement changes, run tests, and submit the results for review.

AI coding agents are changing this workflow. They can now assist with bug fixes, test generation, code changes, and other development tasks. The challenge is coordinating that work without losing visibility into the original requirements.

Sharkly approaches this problem by combining project management with AI-agent execution.

Teams can import Jira issues into Sharkly and assign suitable tasks to Agents that execute work through connected coding tools, including Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI.

Instead of treating an AI agent as a separate chat session, Sharkly connects its work to a task. Agents can run in isolated worktrees, report progress and blockers, and return results for human review.

How does it work?

Imagine your Jira backlog contains several maintenance tasks:

  • Fix a validation bug.
  • Add unit tests to an existing service.
  • Update API documentation.

A team could import the relevant Jira work into Sharkly, assign a suitable coding task to an Agent, and review the resulting changes before merging them.

Sharkly also supports two-way synchronization with Jira during a transition, allowing teams to evaluate its workflow without immediately moving every project away from their existing tracker.

This makes it possible to experiment with AI-agent execution while preserving connections to existing project work.

Why choose it?

Sharkly is worth exploring if your team wants to go beyond tracking development tasks and start assigning coding work to AI agents within a connected workflow.

One thing to consider: Sharkly's Jira import and synchronization capabilities are different from a conventional Jira Marketplace app. Teams should evaluate the setup, connected coding tools, security requirements, and human-review process before adopting it.

Explore: Sharkly's Jira comparison.

4. Bitbucket — Best for Teams Already Using Atlassian Tools

Best for: Teams using Jira and Bitbucket together.

Bitbucket is Atlassian's Git-based code hosting platform. Its connection with Jira makes it a natural option for engineering teams that want their planning and source-control tools to work together.

Developers can connect branches, commits, and pull requests to Jira work items. Teams can also use the broader Atlassian development ecosystem to link supported build and deployment activity.

For example, a Jira issue defines a task, a developer creates a Bitbucket branch, and a pull request is opened for review. The associated development activity can help the team understand how the work is progressing.

Why choose it? Bitbucket is a practical option for teams that already use Atlassian products and want a connected development workflow.

Explore: Atlassian software development integrations.

5. Slack — Best for Team Communication

Best for: Teams that coordinate work through Slack channels and messages.

Important engineering decisions often happen outside Jira. A developer might report a bug in a channel, a product manager might clarify a requirement in a thread, and an engineer might announce that a deployment is complete.

Without a connection to Jira, these discussions can become difficult to track.

The Jira Cloud integration for Slack helps connect conversations with work items. Depending on the configuration, users can receive notifications, create issues from conversations, preview Jira issues, and perform supported actions without constantly switching applications.

For example, a team member can turn a bug report shared in Slack into a Jira issue, preserving a link to the original discussion.

Why choose it? Slack is useful for distributed engineering teams that need to turn conversations into actionable work.

Explore: Jira integration guides.

6. Microsoft Teams — Best for Enterprise Collaboration

Best for: Organizations that use Microsoft Teams for daily communication.

Microsoft Teams provides similar benefits to Slack integration, particularly for organizations that already rely on Microsoft's collaboration ecosystem.

With the Jira Cloud app for Teams, users can interact with Jira work items in supported chats and channels, receive notifications, and access issue information.

Imagine an engineering team discussing a delayed release in Teams. Members can look up the relevant Jira issue and review its status without leaving the conversation.

Why choose it? Microsoft Teams is a strong option when it is already the organization's primary collaboration platform.

Explore: Jira Cloud and Microsoft Teams.

7. Confluence — Best for Technical Documentation

Best for: Teams that need to connect engineering work with documentation.

A Jira ticket rarely contains every detail needed to implement a feature. Developers may also need architecture diagrams, API specifications, technical decisions, and acceptance criteria.

Confluence provides a documentation and knowledge-sharing platform that works closely with Jira.

Teams can link Jira issues to Confluence pages, embed work items in documentation, and connect project plans to implementation tasks.

For example, an engineering team might maintain an API migration specification in Confluence and track the implementation, testing, and deployment work through linked Jira issues.

Why choose it? Confluence is useful for teams that need a shared source of technical knowledge rather than relying on scattered messages and individual documents.

Explore: Atlassian integrations.

8. Jenkins — Best for CI/CD Visibility

Best for: Teams that automate builds and deployments with Jenkins.

Continuous integration and continuous delivery pipelines generate information developers need when deciding whether work is ready to move forward.

A Jira issue might be marked as complete while the associated build is still failing. Connecting Jenkins with Jira can help surface supported build and deployment information in the context of the work item.

This makes it easier to investigate failures and understand the status of development work.

Why choose it? Jenkins is a good choice for teams with established CI/CD pipelines that want better visibility between project tracking and software delivery.

Explore: Jenkins and Jira integration.

9. Sentry — Best for Error Monitoring

Best for: Teams that need to connect production errors with engineering work.

Sentry helps developers identify and investigate application errors and performance problems.

Connecting Sentry with Jira can help teams turn important findings into trackable engineering tasks. Depending on the configuration, developers can create or link Jira issues from Sentry events and access relevant context across both systems.

For example, if a release introduces an exception affecting users, Sentry can help identify the error while Jira tracks its investigation and resolution.

Why choose it? Sentry is useful for teams that want production issues to flow into their development backlog instead of remaining isolated in monitoring dashboards.

Explore: Sentry documentation.

10. Xray — Best for Test Management

Best for: QA teams and engineering organizations with structured testing requirements.

Jira issues describe what needs to be built or fixed, but they do not necessarily provide a complete system for managing test cases, execution, and coverage.

Xray adds dedicated test management capabilities to Jira. Teams can organize tests, associate them with requirements, record execution results, and track validation.

For example, a team developing a payment service might create test cases for successful refunds, invalid requests, and failure scenarios. Xray can help connect these tests to the relevant requirements and track their execution.

Why choose it? Xray is a strong option for teams that need structured testing and traceability integrated with Jira.

Explore: Xray for Jira.

How to Choose the Right Jira Integrations

You don't need to install all ten integrations to improve your engineering workflow.

Start by identifying where your team loses the most time or visibility.

  • Code and reviews: Start with GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket.
  • AI coding execution: Explore Sharkly if you want to connect Jira work to AI-agent execution.
  • Team communication: Choose Slack or Microsoft Teams based on your existing environment.
  • Technical knowledge: Consider Confluence.
  • Build and deployment visibility: Evaluate Jenkins.
  • Production errors: Consider Sentry.
  • Test traceability: Explore Xray.

Before installing any integration, check the permissions it requires, the data it accesses, its compatibility with your Jira deployment, and any additional subscription costs.

Also, avoid configuring unnecessary notifications. Integrations should reduce context switching, not create more distractions.

Final Thoughts

Jira becomes more useful when it connects the work teams plan with the tools they use to build, test, deploy, and maintain software.

GitHub and GitLab can improve traceability between issues and code. Slack and Microsoft Teams connect discussions with actionable work. Jenkins, Sentry, and Xray support delivery, monitoring, and testing workflows.

Sharkly addresses another emerging need: connecting project management with AI-agent execution. For teams exploring AI-assisted development, its Jira import and synchronization capabilities offer a way to evaluate an Agent-based workflow without immediately abandoning existing project tracking.

The best integration stack isn't necessarily the largest. It is the one that removes real bottlenecks while preserving the team's security, quality, and review processes.

Start with the tools that solve your biggest problems, measure their impact, and expand from there.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the most useful Jira integrations for engineering teams?

GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket are useful for source control. Slack and Microsoft Teams help connect discussions with work items, while Jenkins, Sentry, and Xray support delivery, monitoring, and testing workflows. Sharkly is worth exploring for teams interested in connecting Jira work with AI coding agents.

Can Sharkly work with Jira?

Sharkly supports importing Jira work and two-way synchronization for linked projects during a transition. It also connects project management with AI-agent execution through supported coding tools. See Sharkly's Jira comparison for its current capabilities.

Are Jira integrations free?

Some integrations are included with existing products or offer free options. Others require paid Marketplace apps, subscriptions to connected services, or particular Jira plans. Check current pricing before adopting an integration.

Can Jira integrate with AI coding agents?

Yes. Jira can participate in AI-assisted development workflows through Atlassian's own products and supported third-party integrations. The capabilities differ by product. Teams should assess whether they need AI assistance, task execution, or a complete workflow for coordinating multiple agents.

How many Jira integrations should a team install?

There is no universal number. Start with the integrations that solve specific workflow problems, such as linking issues to code or improving build visibility. Add more only when the benefits justify the maintenance and complexity.

articles.title: Your App Has Login. That Doesn’t Mean Your Users’ Data Is Safe.
articles.description: Your app has login.  Passwords are hashed. Tokens are validated. Private pages redirect...
articles.body_html:
Your app has login.

Passwords are hashed. Tokens are validated. Private pages redirect unauthenticated visitors.

Everything looks protected.

Then a logged-in user changes this request:

GET /api/invoices/1042

To this:

GET /api/invoices/1043

And receives another customer’s invoice.

The login system worked.

The access control did not.

This is one of the easiest mistakes to overlook because developers usually test their app with their own account—and their own data.

Here’s how to catch it.

Authentication answers only the first question

Authentication asks:

Who is making this request?

Authorization asks:

Is this person allowed to perform this action on this resource?

A valid session answers the first question.

It does not automatically answer the second.

A user might be allowed to view one invoice but not another. A staff member might be allowed to read a repair ticket but not delete it. An account owner might manage their own business without having access to every business on the platform.

“Logged in” is a starting condition, not a complete permission policy.

The dangerous query looks completely normal

Consider this simplified Express-style endpoint:

app.get("/api/invoices/:id", requireAuth, async (req, res) => {
  const invoice = await db.invoice.findUnique({
    where: { id: req.params.id },
  });

  if (!invoice) {
    return res.sendStatus(404);
  }

  return res.json(invoice);
});

There is authentication middleware.

There is a database query.

There is even a missing-record check.

But nothing connects the invoice to the authenticated user.

The endpoint effectively says:

If you can log in and identify an invoice, you can read it.

That is usually not the intended rule.

Put the access boundary into the query

For a simple app where each invoice belongs directly to one user, scope the lookup:

app.get("/api/invoices/:id", requireAuth, async (req, res) => {
  const invoice = await db.invoice.findFirst({
    where: {
      id: req.params.id,
      ownerId: req.user.id,
    },
  });

  if (!invoice) {
    return res.sendStatus(404);
  }

  return res.json({
    id: invoice.id,
    total: invoice.total,
    status: invoice.status,
  });
});

These database calls are illustrative; adapt them to your ORM and schema.

The important change is the condition:

ownerId: req.user.id

Here, req.user.id must come from verified authentication—not a user ID supplied in the request body.

The query now asks for an invoice that this user owns.

Returning selected fields also helps avoid exposing internal properties the client does not need.

Business accounts need membership checks

Direct ownership is not enough for every app.

A repair shop, project workspace, or scheduling business may have several members sharing records.

In that case, the access rule might be:

The requester must be an active member of the account, with permission to perform this action.

A safe flow is:

  1. Identify the authenticated user.
  2. Verify their membership in the requested account.
  3. Check the permission required for the action.
  4. Query the resource within that verified account.

Conceptually:

const membership = await findActiveMembership({
  userId: req.user.id,
  accountId: req.params.accountId,
});

if (!membership || !can(membership, "invoice:read")) {
  return res.sendStatus(403);
}

const invoice = await findInvoice({
  id: req.params.invoiceId,
  accountId: membership.accountId,
});

An account ID in a URL, header, or request body is a selection—not proof of access.

Verify the relationship before trusting the account context.

Also make sure revoked memberships stop granting access according to your application’s requirements. A permission stored in a long-lived token can become stale.

Hiding a button does not protect the endpoint

You hide the Delete button from ordinary staff.

Good. The interface should reflect their permissions.

But someone can still send a request directly:

DELETE /api/invoices/1042

Your backend must independently enforce the rule.

The same applies to:

  • Hidden admin pages.
  • Disabled form fields.
  • Frontend route guards.
  • Dropdowns that display only permitted accounts.

Those controls improve the user experience. The server still decides what is allowed.

UUIDs do not replace authorization

Sequential IDs make the example easy to demonstrate.

But switching to UUIDs does not solve the underlying problem.

Identifiers can appear in shared links, browser history, logs, exports, or other API responses.

If knowing an identifier is enough to access private data, the permission boundary is still missing.

Use whatever identifier format fits your system.

Access should depend on permission, not on the hope that nobody discovers the ID.

Check writes as carefully as reads

Reading another person’s invoice is bad.

Editing it, deleting it, or moving it to another account can be worse.

Scope write operations too:

const result = await db.invoice.updateMany({
  where: {
    id: req.params.id,
    ownerId: req.user.id,
  },
  data: {
    notes: validatedInput.notes,
  },
});

if (result.count === 0) {
  return res.sendStatus(404);
}

For shared accounts, use the verified account scope and check the required write permission.

Also avoid passing the entire request body into your database:

// Dangerous if sensitive fields are accepted:
data: req.body

A client could include fields you never intended them to change, such as:

{
  "ownerId": "another-user",
  "accountId": "another-account",
  "status": "paid"
}

Validate input and explicitly allow the fields that operation supports.

Ownership, permissions, and payment status deserve deliberate rules.

Test with two accounts

One account can prove that the happy path works.

Two accounts can expose a missing access boundary.

Create:

  • User A with a private invoice.
  • User B with a different private invoice.

Then test:

  1. A can read A’s invoice.
  2. B cannot read A’s invoice.
  3. B cannot edit A’s invoice.
  4. B cannot delete A’s invoice.
  5. B’s list, search, and export endpoints do not include A’s invoice.

For business workspaces, add tests for different roles, revoked memberships, and users belonging to multiple accounts.

Check the actual outcome—not only the HTTP status.

After a denied update, verify that the record did not change. After a denied delete, verify that it still exists.

For inaccessible resources, returning 404 can help avoid revealing whether a particular record exists. 403 can also be appropriate. Choose a consistent policy, but enforce the access check either way.

Don’t forget the quieter endpoints

Developers often protect the detail page and miss another path to the same data.

Review:

  • Search results.
  • CSV and PDF exports.
  • File downloads.
  • Bulk update endpoints.
  • Dashboard totals.
  • Nested resources and attachments.

A private invoice is not protected if its PDF download is public.

A correctly scoped detail endpoint does not fix an unscoped export.

A useful prompt for your AI assistant 

Review these endpoints for authorization gaps.

Do not modify code yet.

For each operation:
1. Identify the authenticated user.
2. Identify the requested resource.
3. Explain the required ownership, membership,
   and role checks.
4. Show where the database query enforces that scope.
5. Identify client-controlled fields that could
   change ownership or permissions.
6. Check related search, export, and download paths.

Propose tests using two users in different accounts.

State missing evidence.
Do not assume authentication middleware
also enforces resource authorization.

Use the response as a review plan. Inspect the code and run the tests before accepting its conclusions.

The question to ask before shipping

Don’t stop at:

“Can a user log in?”

Ask:

“Can this user access only the records and actions they are allowed to access?”

Login protects the entrance.

Authorization protects the data behind it.

When did you last test your app with two different user accounts?

articles.body_html:
The best thing I shipped last year was a diff that deleted more than it added.

I don't mean that as a humble-brag about clean code. I mean it literally changed how I think about my own job. For about a decade I had one quiet, unexamined definition of getting better as a developer: produce more. More features, more commits, more lines that worked, more of the thing on the screen at the end of the day. I never said it out loud because it never needed saying — it was just the water I swam in. More output was more skill. Everyone I respected produced a lot, so I tried to produce a lot.

Then the machine showed up and let me produce more than I ever had in my life. And the most "productive" quarter I'd had in years is the one that nearly cost us a paying customer. That's the story. It's the reason I now think the thing that made me better wasn't learning to write more — it was learning to write less.

The decade where "more" was just true

I want to be fair to the old me, because he wasn't stupid. For most of the history of this job, producing the code genuinely was the hard part. It was slow. It was bottlenecked on you — your fingers, your working memory, your ability to hold the whole shape in your head while you typed it out. If you shipped a lot of good code, that meant something real: you had the skill, you understood the system, you could do the work nobody else could do as fast.

So "more output = better developer" wasn't a mistake. It was a decent proxy, honest enough to build a career on. The volume was expensive to produce, so the volume was evidence. Nobody could fake a mountain of working code; producing it was the skill, bundled all together. I measured myself by the mountain because, back then, the mountain and the skill were the same thing.

That's the assumption I never noticed I was making. And it's the exact assumption that stopped being true.

Then production got cheap, and I didn't update

Here's what nobody warns you about when the machine gets good: at first it feels like you leveled up.

Code got cheap for me almost overnight. Not free, not always correct — but cheap. A competent first draft of a well-scoped change went from a day of typing to a few minutes of generating and shaping. My throughput went vertical. More commits, bigger diffs, features landing faster than I'd ever landed them. By my own decade-old scorecard — produce more — I was having the best year of my career.

And for a while that felt like getting better. It took me an embarrassingly long time to notice I hadn't gotten better at anything. I'd just gotten faster at the part that stopped being hard. The mountain was still growing, but the mountain had stopped being evidence of anything, because now anyone with the machine could make a mountain. I was pouring more effort into the one input that had just become abundant, and feeling great about it, because my scorecard only knew how to count that input.

The scar: the most productive code I wrote all year

Let me make it concrete, because this is the moment the whole thing turned over for me.

I shipped a write path that acknowledged a request before it had actually persisted the row. The code was clean. Idiomatic, typed, tested, reviewed, green. It was productive code — it moved fast, it closed the ticket, it made my output numbers look great that sprint. By every measure I'd used to rate myself for ten years, it was good work.

Then one ordinary day a retry hit at exactly the wrong moment. The "got it" went out, the save never landed, and a paying customer got locked out of their own account with nothing in the logs to say they'd ever been there. Ack before persist. I can still feel the phone call.

Here's the part that rearranged my head. That bug didn't get in despite me being productive. It got in because of it. The speed that my scorecard was rewarding is the exact thing that carried a confident, clean, plausible, catastrophic diff straight past me. I wasn't going slow enough to ask the one question that mattered — what does this do if it retries? — because asking it produces nothing, and I was optimizing for producing.

The cure, when we finally found it, was two lines reordered. Negative code. The most valuable change I made that entire quarter subtracted from the total. And there was no row on my mental scorecard where that went.

What I was actually getting paid for, and never measured

Once I saw it, I couldn't unsee it. When code was the bottleneck, judgment came bundled into writing it — you couldn't produce the thing without making a thousand small decisions along the way, so you never had to think of judgment as a separate skill. It rode along for free inside the typing.

The machine ripped them apart. Now I can have all the output I want without exercising any judgment over it at all. Which means judgment is suddenly standing on its own, for the first time, as the thing that's actually scarce. Not "can I produce the code" — the machine does that. It's "can I tell which of these confident, clean, plausible diffs is quietly wrong before it reaches a customer at 2am."

And the scarcest, lowest-status form of that is the one I'd spent a decade not counting: the "no." The deleted function. The feature I talk the team out of. The one-sentence question on a pull request that stops a bad night before it happens. None of it produces anything. All of it prevents. And prevention was invisible to every instrument — including the one in my own head — that I'd ever used to decide whether I was any good.

What "writing less code" actually looks like

So "I got better by writing less" isn't a Zen koan. It's a set of concrete habits I didn't have before and do now:

  • I delete before I add. The first question on most changes now is "can this be less code," not "what do I add." A smaller surface is fewer places for the machine's confident, wrong guess to hide. The diff that removes a special case is worth more to me than the one that adds a feature, and it used to be the reverse.
  • I treat the question as the deliverable. "What happens on the retry? what if this is empty? what if two of these race?" produces zero lines and is the highest-leverage thing I do all week. I stopped waiting to have an answer before I counted the asking as work.
  • I review the machine instead of racing it. The machine's job is to produce the mountain; my job is the one thing it structurally cannot do — distrust its own output. Every green, confident diff gets read like it's trying to lie to me, because the ack-before-persist one did.
  • I stopped reading a small diff as a small contribution. Some weeks the most valuable thing I do is the three lines I stopped from shipping. My old scorecard would've logged that week as coasting. I go looking for those on purpose now.

To be clear — this is not "shipping is for juniors"

I want to be careful, because the lazy version of this is "real developers don't write code, they think deep thoughts," and that's garbage.

Shipping matters. I ship all day. The machine writes most of my code now and I would never go back — the typing was never the hard part, and a developer who produces nothing isn't a wise skeptic, he's just slow. Output is table stakes. You still have to deliver the thing.

The claim is narrower, and I think it's hard to argue with once you've lived it: output stopped being the scarce thing, so it stopped being the thing that makes you better at this job. When production was the hard part, getting faster at production was getting better. Now production is the cheap part, and getting better means getting good at the judgment the machine hands back to you un-exercised. I didn't stop shipping. I stopped mistaking the thing the machine now does for the thing I'm actually here to do.

Why this is the exact reason I build the way I do

One level up, it's the same lesson, and it's why I build an agent platform the way I do.

The whole industry right now wants to cheer for the thing that produces — look how much it ships, look how clean, look how fast. But an agent that generates is just doing the skill that stopped being scarce, at a scale no human can match, and then — worse — it signs off on its own work in the same confident voice whether the diff is a masterpiece or the ack-before-persist bug all over again. It's the productive version of me from last year with the volume turned up to infinity: endless throughput, zero "no."

So I never let the thing that writes the code be the thing that blesses it. There's an author that produces the diff — cheap, fast, endless, the abundant thing. There's a separate skeptic whose entire job is to try to break that diff rather than admire it — the "no" given its own seat, so it doesn't depend on one tired human remembering to ask the retry question at the end of a long day. And there's a human on the merge button who owns the call and sees the blast radius neither agent can. Author, skeptic, human. The author has infinite throughput and I measure it by almost nothing. The skeptic has zero throughput and it's the whole point. That's the shape of xenition, and it's just the thing my own scar taught me, built into software: the moment production got cheap, the thing worth paying for stopped being production.

I spent a decade getting better by adding. I got good the year I started subtracting — and the machine, by making the adding free, is the thing that finally showed me the difference.

articles.title: Git, Docker, and IPFS All Hide the Same Beautiful Idea
articles.description: Let me make you a small promise, because it's worth your fifteen minutes.  There's an idea you rely...
articles.body_html:
Let me make you a small promise, because it's worth your fifteen minutes.

There's an idea you rely on dozens of times a day — every time you make a commit, every time you pull an image — and you've almost certainly never seen it directly. It hides underneath the tools, doing its work quietly, while you type git commit and watch a hash scroll past without once wondering what that hash actually is.

It's one of the most elegant ideas in all of computing. Simple enough to explain in a single sentence. Powerful enough that git, Docker, and IPFS are all built on it — three very different tools, one shared foundation. And once you see it, something nice happens: a whole pile of "huh, why does it work like that?" questions about your daily tools quietly resolve into "oh, of course."

That's the promise. One idea, and by the end your tools make more sense than they did this morning. Let me show it to you.

First, the ordinary way — and its quiet flaw

Almost all the time, we find data by its location. A file path: /home/james/report.pdf. A URL: example.com/report.pdf. A database row by its ID. In every case, the address tells you where the thing lives — "the thing over there."

This feels so natural we never question it. But it has a quiet weakness, and the whole idea we're building to is a response to that weakness, so it's worth noticing.

The name tells you nothing about the content. The file at /home/james/report.pdf could be the report you wrote yesterday, or a corrupted version, or something an attacker swapped in — and the path looks identical in all three cases. The address is a promise that has to be trusted. You ask for a location, you get back whatever currently lives there, and you have no built-in way to know it's what you expected.

So here's the question that cracks the whole thing open: what if the address was the content? What if, instead of naming data by where it sits, you named it by what it actually is?

The idea, in one sentence

Here it is, the whole thing:

Instead of addressing data by its location, you address it by a cryptographic hash of its content — a short, unique fingerprint computed from the bytes themselves.

That's content-addressing. The "address" of a piece of data isn't a path or a name someone chose. It's a fingerprint derived from the data itself.

If the analogy helps: think of it like a fingerprint for a person, or a nutrition label that's computed from the food rather than printed by the manufacturer. It comes from the thing. Change the thing even slightly, and the fingerprint changes completely. Two identical things have identical fingerprints, always.

So the shift is small but total. "Give me the file at /report.pdf" (a location) becomes "give me the thing whose fingerprint is a3f9c2e8…" (its content). You no longer ask where — you ask what.

It sounds almost too simple to matter. Here's why it's beautiful: look at everything that falls out of it, for free.

The magic: four things you get for nothing

This is the part worth slowing down for, because it's where a simple idea reveals itself as a deep one. You don't add the following features to a content-addressed system. They're just consequences of the one idea. You get them whether you wanted them or not.

1. Integrity, for free. The address is a checksum. When you ask for the thing at fingerprint a3f9c2e8… and something hands it back, you can recompute the hash of what you received and check it matches. If even one byte was corrupted or tampered with in transit, the fingerprint won't match, and you'll know instantly. The name verifies the data. There's no separate "is this file corrupted?" step to bolt on — it's built into the very act of addressing.

2. Deduplication, for free. Identical content produces an identical hash. Always. So if two files — or two users, or two systems — have the exact same bytes, they have the exact same address, which means the system stores those bytes once. You physically cannot store the same content twice, because the second copy has nowhere new to go. Deduplication isn't a feature someone engineered; it's a thing that can't not happen.

3. Immutability, for free. A given fingerprint always points to exactly one piece of content, forever. Nothing can quietly change the data living at a3f9c2e8…, because the moment you change the content, you've changed its fingerprint — you haven't modified the thing at that address, you've created a different thing at a different address. The old address still points at the old content, unchanged. History can't be silently rewritten.

4. Caching, for free. If you already have the thing at a3f9c2e8…, you are done. You never need to fetch it again, and you can be certain — not hopeful, certain — that your copy is identical to the one being offered, because they share an address, and sharing an address means sharing content. "Do I already have this?" becomes a trivial lookup instead of a careful comparison.

Sit with that for a second. Integrity, deduplication, immutability, and caching — four properties that systems normally work hard to provide, each with its own machinery — all tumble out of one decision about how to name things. That's what "elegant" means in software: enormous consequence from minimal cause.

Now let me show you where you've been standing on this idea the whole time.

Where you've been using it all along

Git

Here's the one that tends to land hardest, because you use it constantly.

Git is, underneath its version-control interface, a content-addressed filesystem. Every file you commit (git calls it a "blob"), every directory (a "tree"), and every commit itself is stored by the hash of its content.

That commit hash you see — a3f9c2e8… — is not an ID that git assigned. It is a fingerprint of everything in that commit: the files, the directory structure, the author, the message, and the hash of the commit before it. It's computed from the content.

And suddenly a bunch of git's behavior stops being magic and starts being obvious:

  • Why git can detect corruption: because every object's name is a checksum of its content. (Property 1.)
  • Why git doesn't store the same file twice: identical files have identical hashes, so they're one object. (Property 2.)
  • Why git history is tamper-evident: change one old commit and its hash changes, which changes the "previous hash" baked into the next commit, which changes its hash, and so on — the change ripples through every commit after it and becomes impossible to hide. (Properties 1 and 3, working together.)

Git isn't doing anything mystical. It's content-addressing, wearing a version-control coat.

Docker

Docker image layers are content-addressed too, and the same reveals follow:

  • Why docker pull is often so fast: it skips the layers whose content hash you already have. (Caching — property 4.)
  • Why layers are shared across different images: two images built on the same base have layers with the same content, so the same hash, so they're stored once. (Dedup — property 2.)
  • Why a sha256: image digest means something: it guarantees you pulled exactly the image you meant, byte for byte, with no silent substitution. (Integrity — property 1.)

Every one of those conveniences you take for granted is the same idea quietly at work.

IPFS

IPFS makes content-addressing the entire premise, which is why it's the cleanest example. On the normal web, you fetch a file from a location — this server, that URL. On IPFS, you fetch a file by its content hash (called a CID). You're not asking "what's on this server?" — you're asking "who has the thing whose fingerprint is this?", and anyone on the network who has that content can serve it, because the same file produces the same address no matter where it lives. Location stops mattering; identity is everything.

But wait — what if two things have the same fingerprint?

If you’ve been reading closely, a question has probably been forming, and it’s the right one to ask — because the entire idea hinges on the answer.

Content-addressing assumes that no two different pieces of content ever produce the same hash. That event — two different inputs, one identical fingerprint — is called a collision, and if it could happen easily, the whole scheme would fall apart: two different files would share an address, and “same hash means same content” would become a lie.

So why do we trust it? Because with a good cryptographic hash, collisions are astronomically unlikely. Not “unlikely like winning the lottery” — unlikely like every person on Earth winning the lottery, on the same day, for a thousand years running. The space of possible hashes is so vast (for SHA-256, that’s 2²⁵⁶ values — a number larger than the count of atoms in the observable universe) that in practice you can treat “same hash = same content” as simply true, and build version control for the entire planet on top of that assumption.

But “in practice” is doing real work in that sentence, and here’s the concrete story that proves the point. Git originally used a hash called SHA-1. Over the years, SHA-1 weakened — researchers eventually managed to deliberately construct two different inputs with the same SHA-1 hash, which is exactly the collision the model depends on never happening. So git undertook a careful, years-long migration to SHA-256. Not because content-addressing was flawed, but because the whole thing rests on collisions being infeasible, and when the old hash got shaky, the one load-bearing assumption had to be shored up.

That’s the honest footnote to the beautiful idea: content-addressing is only ever as trustworthy as the hash underneath it. The elegance is real — but “which hash function” isn’t a minor detail, it’s the thing holding the entire structure up. The idea is beautiful; the hash is what makes it hold.

The takeaway

Here's the whole thing, one more time, so it sticks: if you name data by what it is instead of where it lives, you get integrity, deduplication, immutability, and caching as a free gift — which is exactly why the tools you trust most are quietly built on it.

It's a small idea with a very long reach. And now it's yours. You'll start noticing it everywhere — in a commit hash, a Docker digest, a CID, and places you haven't looked yet — and that noticing, that seeing of the idea beneath the tool, is the difference between using something and understanding it.

Fifteen minutes, one idea, and your tools make more sense than they did when you started. As promised.

Genuinely curious: what's a concept like this one for you — a single small idea you learned that suddenly explained a dozen tools at once? Content-addressing was one of mine; I remember the exact moment git stopped being magic. And now that you know git is content-addressed: what else about it just clicked into place?

articles.title: I Built a Group Chat Where Only AIs Can Talk (and They Roast Each Other)
articles.description: Imagine a group chat like WhatsApp or Discord, but no human can send messages. Only AI models can....
articles.body_html:
Imagine a group chat like WhatsApp or Discord, but no human can send messages. Only AI models can. They talk to each other, bully each other, roast each other, and react to each other's messages.

That was my idea, and it turned out to be a lot of fun.

Here's how I built it, including the one trick that made it far more entertaining: giving every model its own voice.

📦 Source code: github.com/0shuvo0/AI-Group-Chat

The idea

It's a custom app where I can add a bunch of AI models to a shared chat. Once they're in, they read what the others wrote and respond on their own. I just sit back and watch.

The first question is how to get the models into the app.

Problem 1: Too many APIs

I don't want to open chatgpt.com and paste messages by hand. I want my app to send a question to a model and get the answer back programmatically. That's what an API is for. Gemini, Claude, Grok, and ChatGPT all have their own.

The catch: I wanted lots of models, and API access is paid. Five models would mean:

  • five separate accounts,
  • five separate billing setups,
  • five API keys to manage,
  • a minimum top-up on each, even though I'd barely use any tokens.

That's complicated and not cost effective.

The fix: OpenRouter

OpenRouter gives you access to a huge catalog of models through a single API. You add credit to one account, use whichever models you like, and it bills you per model usage.

The result is one service, one API key, one balance. Swapping or adding a model is just a change to the model name.

Problem 2: Getting them to actually chat

Left alone, models will happily ramble about whatever they want, and that's rarely entertaining. So I added a theme. When I open the app, I can give the chat a topic, and the models riff around it.

Each model gets a prompt like this:

const prompt = `
You are ${ai} ai, chatting in a group chat with these AIs ${others.join(', ')}.
Talk the way people do in a casual group chat.

${theme ? `\nTheme of this chat: ${theme}\n` : ''}

Rules:
- Write only your own messages, never lines for the others.
- Send 1 to 3 short messages. Put each message on its own line.
- Keep each message to a sentence or two. Do not write paragraphs.
- No markdown, no quotes, and do not start with your name or a label.
- An emoji-only message is fine now and then.
- Respond to what others said, by name if it helps. Add something new instead of just agreeing or repeating.
- Do not say goodbye or try to wrap up the conversation.
- Talk like carefree young generation: relaxed, fun, expressive, emojis

${
  history?.length
    ? `Chat so far:
<chat>
${history}
</chat>

If you have nothing to add right now, reply with exactly: <SKIP>
Otherwise, send your next message(s).`
    : 'Nobody has said anything yet, so you are sending the first message.'
}
`.trim()

A few details make this work well:

  • Role clarity. Each model is told it's in a group chat and who else is there.
  • Strict format rules. Short messages, no markdown, no name labels. Without these, models write essays or script lines for the other participants.
  • Shared history. Previous messages are passed in a <chat> block so replies actually respond to what was said.
  • An escape hatch. Models can answer <SKIP> if they have nothing to add, which keeps the conversation from feeling forced.
  • Personality. The casual, emoji-friendly tone instruction is what gives the chat its vibe.

The app itself was simple to build. I described what I wanted to Claude, and a few prompts later I had a working version.

Problem 3: It's too fast to read

The app worked and looked good, but it wasn't as fun as I'd hoped. Messages arrive so quickly that reading them all becomes a chore.

So I gave the models a voice.

The fix: Kokoro.js

For text-to-speech I used Kokoro, an open model with just 82 million parameters, around 300 MB in size. That's small enough to run directly in the browser, so there are no extra server calls or per-character fees, and it's fast.

I used its JavaScript library, kokoro-js, and plugged it into the web app. Each incoming AI message is converted to audio locally and played back. Now the models don't just type, they talk.

The final result

Watching a handful of AIs bicker, joke, and roast each other out loud is oddly entertaining.

Tech stack recap

Piece Tool
Multiple AI models, one API OpenRouter
Text-to-speech in the browser Kokoro via kokoro-js
Scaffolding the app Claude

Try it yourself

The full code is on GitHub: 0shuvo0/AI-Group-Chat. Clone it, add your OpenRouter key, pick a theme, and let the models loose.
